extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, constitutional history, and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-level survey of the historical development, types, tendencies, and practical effects of United States state constitutions from 1776 through the late 19th/early 20th century. It summarizes characteristic features, regional differences, and the practical problems arising from constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-period features: legislative supremacy and weak executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the early (c.1776–c.1806) State Constitutions manifest a dread of executive and military power and a disposition to leave everything to the legislature; election of the State governor is in most States vested in the legislature; the governor is nominally assisted but in reality checked by a council not of his own choosing; he generally had no veto on Acts of the legislature and no right of adjourning or dissolving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why early constitutions consisted largely of an elaborate Bill of Rights and a simple government outline with a representative legislature and carefully separated executive officers and courts. Notes exceptions (e.g., Massachusetts; early New York gave a veto to governor and judges acting together).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-period democratization: popular election and expanded suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first half of the 19th century constitutions moved toward democratization: constitutions began to be directly enacted by popular vote; election of governors was transferred from the legislature to the people; property qualifications were abolished; suffrage became practically universal (with racial exclusions in many places); judges were increasingly chosen by popular vote for fixed terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how constitutions came to embody ordinary law and how the legislature began to be seen as an agent with delegated powers requiring popular recourse for expansion (amendment). Indicates the period's causes (westward settlement, Revolutionary generation influence, French republican ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-period features: strengthened executive/judiciary and fettered legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Since about the Civil War a reaction strengthened executive and judicial departments relative to the legislature: governors obtained veto power in almost every State; gubernatorial tenure and re-eligibility restrictions were often relaxed; judges’ salaries and terms were increased and in some cases judicial appointments shifted to the executive. Meanwhile the legislature's competence was narrowed and its action fettered by complicated restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes that restraining legislatures by constitutional restrictions may, in practice, have conservative results because direct legislation by the people is slower and legislatures are prone to transient popular clamor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency for constitutions to grow longer and more minute
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal modern tendency is for state constitutions to become much longer and more detailed, dealing not only with governmental structure but with education, private law, railroads, municipal indebtedness, judicial and legislative procedure, and an expanding list of matters withdrawn from legislative competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides empirical examples of growth in textual length (e.g., Virginia, Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana) and notes that increased length results both from adding new topics and from treating old topics in greater detail. Suggests possible future direction toward enumerated legislative competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutionalization of ordinary and administrative law
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern constitutions often embody a mass of ordinary private and administrative law—matters formerly left to statutes—by prescribing detailed provisions on subjects such as education, private law, railroads, and the judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns this mixture of fundamental law with ordinary statutory matters creates inconvenience and unscientific confusion, heightening questions of legislative competence and increasing constitutional litigation; it also makes correcting mistakes or omissions harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional types and institutional differences (colonial, Southern, Western)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three formerly distinguishable types: the old colonial/New England type (older middle States), the Southern or Slave State type (influenced by Virginia), and the new or Western type. Older States' constitutions (New England) date earlier and are less minute; newer Southern/Western constitutions are later and more detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes concrete institutional patterns: older States often have stronger executives, judges named by governor rather than elected, unequal electoral districts, and less frequent need to recur to the people; newer States show more similarity among themselves despite variety in details, reflecting common post-1865 tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions reflect local social and economic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State constitution is the work of an independent body that may organize government to suit peculiar conditions and reflect the character of its population; hence constitutions differ according to the social and economic environment of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why newer communities (without a reverent past) change constitutions more frequently, and why social/economic upheavals (e.g., Civil War, end of slavery, rapid population/wealth growth) drive constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct legislation by the people and constitutional directives to legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing practice is to put into the constitution matters proper for ordinary statute and to include directions to the legislature to legislate in a certain sense or for certain purposes, thereby invoking direct popular lawmaking and prescribing legislative aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies practical difficulties: the people cannot be expected to distinguish properly between matters fit for a constitution and for statute; this blurs fundamental and ordinary law, embarrasses the legislature by raising competence questions, and produces abundant constitutional litigation over ultra vires statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability versus frequency of constitutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency of constitutional change varies widely: some States (often newer ones) alter constitutions frequently, while older, well-settled, historic communities tend to maintain constitutions longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides numerical examples (Louisiana 7 constitutions, Virginia/Georgia/South Carolina 6 each, Connecticut/Rhode Island/Maine one each) and suggests two main causes: (1) attachment to habit and historic pride in older communities; (2) rapid economic and social changes in some regions prompting constitutional alteration. Notes average constitutional duration estimated ~30 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of private property and limits on legislative encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions commonly provide safeguards for private property: prohibitions on taking property without due compensation and against special private or personal statutes unfairly affecting individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out that the people's sovereignty has not been used to override private rights generally; exceptions exist for monopolies and wealthy corporations, which are treated differently (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion and regulation of corporations and monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Newer constitutions often single out corporations and monopolies for special treatment: special taxation, limits on duration, restrictions on corporate rights in courts, prohibitions on trustees investing in corporate securities, and measures to check trusts and railroad/warehouse/grain-elevator abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples: Illinois (1870) provisions on grain elevators and railroads; Michigan and Mississippi limit corporate duration; Oklahoma denies ordinary citizen rights to corporations; newer Western constitution provisions multiply to hold corporations in check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of State administrative activity and creation of regulatory bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent constitutions show a tendency to extend public administrative activity by establishing bodies such as railroad commissions, bureaux of agriculture, labour offices, mining commissioners, land registration offices, dairy and insurance commissioners, and agricultural/mining colleges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that, unlike many European states, U.S. States typically do not own railways or mines, but they increasingly regulate these sectors through statutory and constitutional creation of regulatory agencies. Legislative action has been expanding administrative activity as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanitarian and social-welfare clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many constitutions direct establishment of charitable and reformatory institutions, legislation to protect children, comfortable prisons, and homes or farms as asylums for the aged and unfortunate; lotteries are often stringently prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced by provisions excluding convicted persons from the franchise; footnotes cite examples such as prohibitions on child labour under certain ages and restrictions on employment of women/girls in mines in some States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional labor protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Some recent constitutions include labor protections: declaring an eight-hour day lawful on State and municipal works (Wyoming, California, Utah, Idaho), forbidding the letting out of convict labour, prohibiting contracts that escape employer liability for work accidents, and abolishing employer non-liability (in specified sectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mississippi (1890) abolished the employer non-liability doctrine regarding railroads; child-labor prohibitions are specified in certain constitutions (footnoted examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability and practical effectiveness of constitutional provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though constitutions are the supreme law, their provisions are not always better observed or enforced than ordinary statutes; constitutional penalties sometimes fail to achieve their intended social results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates with example of duelling: many constitutions disqualify duellists from office or franchise, yet practices of private violence continued in some States; also notes cases where constitutional penalties or prohibitions (e.g., lotteries) were ignored in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-corruption provisions and disqualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Many constitutions contain explicit anti-corruption measures: oaths by legislators and officers against receiving consideration for votes; making giving/receiving bribes a felony; declaring log-rolling to be bribery; oath requirements about free railroad passes; and criminalizing lobbying in some States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York amendments of 1874 and Constitution of 1894 strengthened such provisions; North Dakota, Montana, Wyoming declare log-rolling bribery; California makes lobbying a felony; South Dakota and Kentucky have specific oaths/provisions concerning free passes and acceptance of favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on federal officials holding State office (state-federal separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: By most state constitutions a Federal official is made incapable not only of State office but also of being a member of a State legislature, reflecting a pronounced jealousy of the Federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prohibitions are often the only references to the National government in state constitutions; states also treat out-of-state (other States') corporations as 'foreign' and sometimes impose special burdens on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional limits on local authorities' borrowing and public works
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions commonly witness a distrust of local authorities—rural as well as urban—by strictly limiting their powers of borrowing or undertaking public works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of a broader tendency to guard against abuses of power at local levels; these limits reflect popular suspicion of both legislative and local officials and aim to protect taxpayers and property holders.
